title: When Have I Done Enough?
opening: I know how to do something. I am much less certain that I know when to stop.
prayer: Lord, I know that my Vindicator lives. Help me remember that when I cannot see what You are doing. Give me wisdom to recognize what You have placed in my hands and courage to act when I should. But when I have done what is mine to do, help me stop trying to control what belongs to You. I will still question. I will still worry. I may still reach for the phone when I should put it down. Keep teaching me the difference between faithfulness and restlessness. I do not want to bargain with You, control the outcome, or measure whether my faith is enough. I want to love You, do the work You give me, and trust You with the rest. Amen.
theme: Knowing when faith asks us to act and when it asks us to release what we cannot control.
body:
I keep thinking about Job alongside the readings of the past few days. Nathanael actually sees Jesus. He meets Him, speaks with Him, and discovers that Jesus knew him before Nathanael ever saw Him. Jesus looks at him and says there is no duplicity in him.
Job doesn't get that encounter. At least not yet. He cannot see God, and still he remains steadfast.
That becomes even more remarkable when I think about the beginning of Job. Satan has been roaming the earth and challenges Job's faithfulness. Is Job faithful only because God has blessed him? Take everything away and what will remain?
Everything about that scene makes me uncomfortable. But Job's response is what stays with me. He loses so much. He suffers. He questions. He pleads his case. Yet today, from within all of that pain, he says, “I know that my Vindicator lives.”
He still doesn't know why.
He just knows God.
Yesterday's Gospel gave us people willing to follow Jesus, but first they had something else to do. I will follow You, but...
Job doesn't give God the but.
Then today Jesus sends the seventy-two out. They go in pairs with almost nothing. They are given work to do, but they are not given control over what happens when they do it. Some will receive them. Others will not. Jesus doesn't tell them to remain until they have convinced everyone. They do what they were sent to do and continue on.
Maybe this is where these readings are meeting me.
I don't want to be the “but.” I don't want to love God because of what He gives me or stop trusting Him because of what has been taken away. Loving Him is enough for me.
But then I wonder whether I actually know how to live that.
Because left to myself, I meddle.
I try to line things up. I make the phone call. I explain my position. Then I explain it again because maybe I wasn't understood. I try to anticipate what could go wrong and do something now so that it doesn't. I advocate. I plan. I try to make an uncertain outcome a little more predictable.
And some of that I have to do. Job argued his case too. Faith does not mean becoming passive when something requires our action.
But when have I done enough?
When does responsibility quietly become restlessness? When does advocating become trying to control the outcome? When am I doing what God has given me to do, and when am I reaching for what was never mine to control?
I don't always know.
Maybe that is why today's Gospel matters. The seventy-two were sent to work, not to control the harvest.
There is something there I need to learn.
Do the work that is mine. Make the call that needs to be made. Speak when something needs to be said. Correct what I reasonably can. Then recognize the moment when I have reached the edge of what belongs to me.
And stop.
That last part is difficult.
Because doing something feels safer than doing nothing. Another phone call feels like movement. Another explanation feels as though I am protecting the outcome. Letting go can feel dangerously close to neglecting something I should have done.
Maybe surrender isn't doing nothing. Maybe it is knowing when I have done what is mine and refusing to take responsibility for what comes next.
Job couldn't control his circumstances. The seventy-two couldn't control how they would be received. Nathanael couldn't control what Jesus already knew about him.
But they were seen by God.
That brings me some peace because maybe I don't need everyone else to understand me perfectly. I should speak truthfully. I should advocate when necessary. I should do the work placed before me. But I cannot make another person understand, agree, decide correctly, or give me the outcome I think should happen.
God sees what they may not.
I also don't want this to become another measurement of my faith. I don't want to start asking whether I have surrendered enough, trusted enough, prayed enough, or somehow failed God because I still feel the urge to pick up the phone.
I don't think Job's faithfulness was the absence of struggle.
He struggled tremendously.
And still:
“I know that my Vindicator lives.”
Maybe that is enough for me today.
I don't know how everything will work out. I don't know when acting becomes meddling. I don't always know whether I am holding something because God has given it to me to handle or because I am afraid of what will happen if I put it down.
But I can ask.
What is mine to do?
I will do that.
What is not mine?
God, help me leave it with You.
